question.text: How can you answer 'have I seen this item before?' using much less memory than a hash set, and what does it cost in accuracy?
question.known_at: Title (line 1), made concrete in the lede (line 5) and the memory paragraph (line 8)
question.result_stated: Yes. Line 5: "So the filter can be wrong in one direction only: it can say 'probably seen' for an item it never saw." Line 8: "takes 1.25 MB (10 bits per URL) and gives a wrong 'probably seen' for 0.82% of new URLs."

reply.motive: Reason to care: "The motive is memory. A hash set of 1 million URLs... takes about 50 MB. A Bloom filter... takes 1.25 MB" (line 8), and the use case "Put the filter in front of a slow exact lookup" (line 77). Reason for the approach: "The memory does not depend on how long the items are, because the filter never keeps them" (line 8). The reason for using several hash functions is given at lines 59-67.
reply.close: Yes. Line 81: "A Bloom filter answers 'have I seen this before?' by remembering only the bits each item turned on. A 0 bit proves an item is new. All 1s mean 'probably seen', which is wrong at a rate p ≈ f^k that you choose with bits per item, and that rises when you add more items than the capacity."
reply.recap: A Bloom filter stores only a few bits per item instead of the items themselves, so it can say 'definitely new' with certainty but only 'probably seen' otherwise; at about 10 bits per item that guess is wrong under 1% of the time.
reply.strongest: Lines 37-44: the owl example reuses cat's and dog's bits to produce a false positive. It then shows, with the same bits, why deleting cat would create a false negative. Both claims are made concrete with no new machinery.
reply.weakest: Line 67: three results arrive in a row with no reason given (best k = (m/n)·ln 2, half the bits are 1 at the best k, and 4.8 bits per item gives 10× lower p). This comes right after a step-by-step derivation that justified every step.
suggestions: At line 67, give a one-line reason: for fixed m/n, p = f^k is smallest when f = 1/2. Then k = (m/n)·ln 2, and p ≈ 0.5^k ≈ 0.6185^(m/n), which gives 4.8 bits per 10× reduction.
At line 8, add a short '(derived below)' after 0.82%.
In the Overfilling section, mention that m is chosen from the expected n and a target p, or move the sizing formula there.
